A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UNI research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison; retained material can be matched despite renumbering and layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-C attribution experiments, including MuFidelity, path monotonicity, adversarial robustness and appendix visual analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds deletion/insertion results, baseline-specificity measurements, a Gaussian-mixture demonstration and language-model attribution experiments.

M1.justification: The image-attribution algorithm remains unchanged. Appendix A.2 adds a bounded methodological extension, UNI-ATTR: it constructs baselines in continuous token-embedding space and uses activation differences and gradients to attribute internal activations, as defined in Equation 6.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained ImageNet coverage, v2 evaluates internal attribution in generative language models using counterfactual prompts from Meng et al. (2023). This introduces a different domain and attribution task. Section 4.3 also adds a synthetic three-point Gaussian-mixture scenario.

E2.justification: The existing vision comparator sets are retained, including in the added deletion/insertion evaluation. Appendix A.2 introduces a comparison between UNI and random baselines for attribution patching, with activation patching serving as the reference in Table 8 and Figure 9. Newly discussed methods such as FORGrad are not reported as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds deletion/insertion AUC evaluation using 10% pixel increments over 10,000 images, and baseline assessment using confidence changes and LPIPS. The NLP protocol measures residual-stream attribution distance from activation patching over 100 prompts on three language models. These are additional evaluation designs; the original vision hyperparameters and FGSM protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 6 add a Gaussian-mixture case study examining baseline proximity, path behavior and full-output matching. Appendix A.1 adds an explicit cross-model specificity analysis using shared inputs, confidence reductions and perceptual distances. The original corruption, adversarial-robustness and Riemann-step analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Existing uncertainty entries are unchanged, and the new vision tables reuse the existing ± presentation without defining an additional statistical procedure. Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts or significance tests. Averaging the NLP results over 100 prompts specifies a sample count, not repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: The original numerical tables are retained, with robustness Tables 3–4 becoming Tables 5–6. New Tables 3–4 rank UNI highest for insertion AUC on all six models; AGI has lower deletion AUC on EfficientNet and ViT. Table 7 adds confidence reductions and LPIPS measurements. Table 8 reports lower attribution-patching distance with UNI than random baselines, including 3.12 versus 6.64 for Pythia. These are added results, not improvements over v1 under previously reported settings.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 replaces the stronger monotonicity argument with a weak sign-consistency condition, removing the gradient-magnitude inequality and the local argument linking nonmonotonic paths to failure of completeness. The Riemann-error bound remains unchanged. Appendix A.2 adds mathematical definitions for activation patching and its attribution approximations, without new proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain the same central claims about static-baseline biases, unlearned baselines and curvature-related robustness. The conclusion reiterates these claims; its additional discussion chiefly develops future applications and research directions.

C2.justification: The new Gaussian-mixture discussion explains why matching the full output vector can select a better baseline than matching target confidence alone, and why proximity normalization matters. Appendix A.1 interprets attribution differences through architectural inductive biases. Appendix A.2 discusses the faithfulness/scalability tradeoff in patching, while the conclusion expands the interpretation of unlearning as a tool for studying feature hierarchies.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies that MuFidelity samples 25% of pixels; the cited 20% concerns prior work, not a documented v1 setting. It also supplies concrete procedures for the added evaluations and states that NLP baseline optimization operates on embeddings without tuning UNI hyperparameters. The original algorithm settings remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Appendix A.2 substantially extends positioning into mechanistic interpretability, relating UNI to activation patching, attribution patching, circuit discovery and IG-based alternatives. Section 6 also adds discussion of Sobol, FORGrad and HSIC, including possible complementarity with UNI. These are substantive additions beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 shortens the title, makes local language and cross-reference corrections, adds Section 4.3, and organizes the appendix into A.1–A.3. The conclusion is expanded, but the document is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds four tables and three figures covering intervention scores, Gaussian-mixture behavior, model specificity and NLP patching. Existing figures are retained and renumbered; several appendix attribution grids are enlarged. The larger grids improve visibility, although some captions now overlap page numbers.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central faithfulness and baseline claims: v1 relied on MuFidelity and visual evidence, whereas v2 adds direct deletion/insertion testing with a stated sampling protocol and quantitative checks of baseline confidence reduction and proximity. The Gaussian-mixture example also clarifies the matching mechanism. The NLP extension remains preliminary, and the weakened theoretical discussion is not fully reconciled with the retained completeness claim, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical validation.
